questions.prompt: What does the acronym ARC stand for in Swift?

options.text: Automatic Reference Counting.
options.explanation: Right. ARC stands for Automatic Reference Counting.

options.text: Asynchronous Resource Control.
options.explanation: ARC is not about asynchronous resource control.

options.text: Automated Runtime Collector.
options.explanation: Swift does not have a runtime garbage collector.

options.text: Allocated Retention Counter.
options.explanation: This is an incorrect expansion of the acronym.

questions.prompt: Which Swift types are managed by Automatic Reference Counting?

options.text: Only standard integer numbers, floating point numbers, and strings.
options.explanation: Integers and floating point numbers are value types on the stack.

options.text: Reference types like classes, actors, and closures.
options.explanation: Right. ARC only tracks reference types.

options.text: All Swift data types including custom structs and enumerations.
options.explanation: Value types like structs and enums do not use reference counts.

options.text: Only Swift structs that conform to the Identifiable protocol.
options.explanation: Conforming to Identifiable does not turn a struct into a reference type.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Automatic Reference Counting

questions.prompt: When is the memory of a class instance freed in Swift?

options.text: When the operating system sends a low memory alert to the app.
options.explanation: ARC frees memory immediately, not only on low memory warnings.

options.text: When the iOS application is terminated by the user.
options.explanation: Objects are deallocated during runtime as soon as references drop to zero.

options.text: Immediately when its strong reference count drops to zero.
options.explanation: Right. ARC reclaims memory as soon as the strong count reaches zero.

options.text: During periodic background passes run by a garbage collector thread.
options.explanation: Swift does not use a background garbage collector.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Automatic Reference Counting

questions.prompt: What method does Swift call right before freeing a class instance from memory?

options.text: free()
options.explanation: free is a C standard library function, not a Swift deinitializer.

options.text: release()
options.explanation: release is an internal Objective-C method, not the Swift syntax.

options.text: dispose()
options.explanation: dispose is used in other languages like C# and Dart.

options.text: deinit
options.explanation: Right. Swift calls deinit immediately before deallocating the instance.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Automatic Reference Counting

questions.prompt: How does Swift ARC differ from a tracing garbage collector like Java or Go?

options.text: ARC inserts retain and release calls at compile time without runtime pauses.
options.explanation: Right. ARC is deterministic and has no stop-the-world pauses.

options.text: ARC runs a background daemon thread that scans all heap pointers periodically.
options.explanation: Tracing garbage collectors use background threads, not ARC.

options.text: ARC requires the developer to call retain and release manually in Swift code.
options.explanation: Swift does this automatically; manual calls were used in legacy Objective-C.

options.text: ARC only runs when compiling Swift apps in Debug build configurations.
options.explanation: ARC runs in both Debug and Release configurations.

sources.title: WWDC21: ARC in Swift: Basics and beyond

questions.prompt: What is the initial strong reference count of a newly created class instance?

options.text: Zero, until it is assigned to a second variable.
options.explanation: If the count were zero, the instance would be freed immediately.

options.text: One, held by the variable or property that receives it.
options.explanation: Right. Initializing an instance and assigning it creates one strong reference.

options.text: Two, one for the instance and one for its type metadata.
options.explanation: Type metadata is not counted as a strong reference to the instance.

options.text: Unlimited, until ARC determines its lifetime scope.
options.explanation: Reference counts are precise integers starting at 1.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Automatic Reference Counting

questions.prompt: What happens to the reference count when a reference variable is assigned to another variable?

options.text: The reference count stays unchanged because the object is not copied.
options.explanation: Each new strong reference increments the reference count.

options.text: The reference count resets to one for both variables.
options.explanation: The reference count belongs to the instance and increases to two.

options.text: The strong reference count increases by one.
options.explanation: Right. Both variables now point to the same object, so count is 2.

options.text: The instance creates a second independent copy on the heap.
options.explanation: Classes are reference types; assigning them does not copy the instance.

questions.prompt: On which thread does Swift execute the deinit method of an object?

options.text: Always on a dedicated background garbage collection thread.
options.explanation: Swift does not have a dedicated garbage collection thread.

options.text: Always on the main thread, regardless of where the object lived.
options.explanation: Deinit does not automatically switch to the main thread.

options.text: On an arbitrary background thread chosen by Grand Central Dispatch.
options.explanation: Deinit is synchronous and does not dispatch to a random thread.

options.text: On the thread that releases the final strong reference.
options.explanation: Right. Deinit runs synchronously on the thread that drops the count to zero.

questions.prompt: What happens when a struct contains a property of class type?

options.text: ARC tracks the class property while the struct itself remains a value type.
options.explanation: Right. The struct copies its values, and ARC retains the class instance.

options.text: The struct automatically converts into a reference type on the heap.
options.explanation: Structs always remain value types regardless of their properties.

options.text: The Swift compiler produces a compile-time error forbidding class properties.
options.explanation: Structs can freely hold class properties.

options.text: ARC ignores the class property, causing an immediate memory leak.
options.explanation: ARC properly retains and releases the class property.

sources.title: WWDC21: ARC in Swift: Basics and beyond

questions.prompt: What happens if two class instances hold strong references to each other?

options.text: ARC detects the loop and deallocates both instances automatically.
options.explanation: ARC cannot detect retain cycles automatically.

options.text: Their counts never drop to zero, creating a retain cycle and memory leak.
options.explanation: Right. Both instances stay alive in memory because counts stay above zero.

options.text: The Swift compiler throws a compile-time circular reference error.
options.explanation: Retain cycles are runtime occurrences, not compile-time errors.

options.text: The app crashes immediately with an out-of-memory exception.
options.explanation: The app does not crash right away; it silently leaks memory.

questions.prompt: What role does the Swift compiler play in Automatic Reference Counting?

options.text: It deletes all classes and replaces them with stack-allocated structs.
options.explanation: The compiler does not convert class types to structs.

options.text: It runs the app inside a virtual machine to intercept pointer calls.
options.explanation: Swift compiles directly to native code without a virtual machine.

options.text: It analyzes scopes and inserts retain and release calls into the binary.
options.explanation: Right. The compiler inserts retain and release calls at compile time.

options.text: It measures CPU temperature to decide when to release memory.
options.explanation: Memory release depends on reference counts, not hardware temperature.

questions.prompt: What are lexical lifetimes in modern Swift?

options.text: Lifetimes that keep variables alive until the application terminates.
options.explanation: Lexical lifetimes do not extend beyond the enclosing lexical block.

options.text: Lifetimes that restrict class instances to the global main thread only.
options.explanation: Lexical lifetimes apply to all threads and local scopes.

options.text: Lifetimes determined randomly by runtime memory pressure.
options.explanation: Lexical lifetimes are deterministic based on code structure.

options.text: A rule keeping local variables alive until the end of their enclosing scope.
options.explanation: Right. Modern Swift keeps objects alive to the end of their lexical scope.

questions.prompt: What happens when a local variable holding a class instance goes out of scope?

options.text: Its reference count decrements by one.
options.explanation: Right. Exiting the scope releases the reference held by the local variable.

options.text: Its reference count is immediately set to zero.
options.explanation: Other variables may still hold strong references to the instance.

options.text: The instance is moved to the global scope.
options.explanation: Objects are not moved to global scope on exit.

options.text: The instance converts into an optional value.
options.explanation: Going out of scope releases the reference, not changes its type.

questions.prompt: Why is keeping deinit methods lightweight recommended in iOS apps?

options.text: Because Swift terminates the process if deinit takes longer than 1 millisecond.
options.explanation: iOS does not terminate apps for slow deinit unless the watchdog triggers.

options.text: Because deinit runs synchronously and can block UI rendering or animations.
options.explanation: Right. Synchronous deinit on the main thread can cause user interface hitching.

options.text: Because ARC ignores deinit methods that contain more than two statements.
options.explanation: ARC always calls deinit regardless of how many statements it contains.

options.text: Because deinit can only execute arithmetic operations.
options.explanation: Deinit can execute standard clean-up code.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Automatic Reference Counting

questions.prompt: In multithreaded Swift code, what overhead do reference count updates introduce?

options.text: They cause deadlocks whenever two background threads run simultaneously.
options.explanation: Atomic increments do not cause deadlocks on their own.

options.text: They pause all worker threads until the main thread approves the allocation.
options.explanation: Worker threads allocate and release memory independently.

options.text: They use atomic operations, which add minor CPU synchronization cost.
options.explanation: Right. Atomic instructions maintain thread safety at small performance cost.

options.text: They force all class instances to be copied to every core.
options.explanation: Instances are shared on the heap; they are not copied across cores.

questions.prompt: Explain what Automatic Reference Counting (ARC) is in Swift and what types it manages. Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that ARC tracks reference counts to determine when to free memory.
Identifies that ARC manages reference types like classes and actors, not value types.
Mentions that deallocation happens immediately when the strong count drops to zero.

questions.modelAnswer: Automatic Reference Counting (ARC) manages memory in Swift by tracking active strong references to instances. It only applies to reference types, such as classes, actors, and closures. When an instance has zero strong references remaining, ARC immediately frees its heap memory.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Automatic Reference Counting

questions.prompt: Compare Swift Automatic Reference Counting with a runtime tracing garbage collector like the one in Java or Go. Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that ARC operates deterministically by inserting retain/release calls at compile time.
Contrasts ARC with tracing garbage collection which runs background scans with potential runtime pauses.
Notes that ARC cannot automatically detect or resolve strong reference cycles.

questions.modelAnswer: Swift ARC inserts retain and release calls at compile time, freeing objects immediately when their count reaches zero without runtime pauses. In contrast, tracing garbage collectors run background threads that periodically scan the heap, which can cause unpredictable latency. However, ARC cannot resolve cyclic references automatically, while tracing garbage collectors can detect disconnected cycles.

sources.title: WWDC21: ARC in Swift: Basics and beyond

questions.prompt: Explain what causes an object reference count to increase and decrease during execution. Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Identifies actions that increase reference count, such as initialization, variable assignment, or property storage.
Identifies actions that decrease reference count, such as setting a variable to nil or leaving scope.
States that the count tracks strong references specifically.

questions.modelAnswer: An object strong reference count increases when it is initialized, assigned to another variable, or stored in a property. The count decreases when a referring variable is set to nil, reassigned, or exits its scope. ARC specifically monitors these strong references to determine object lifetime.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Automatic Reference Counting

questions.prompt: Describe what occurs when a class instance strong reference count reaches zero. Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Swift immediately executes the instance deinit deinitializer.
States that the instance heap memory is immediately returned to the system.
Mentions that deinit executes synchronously on the thread releasing the final reference.

questions.modelAnswer: When an instance strong reference count drops to zero, Swift immediately calls its deinit deinitializer. This runs synchronously on whichever thread dropped the final reference. Once deinit completes, Swift reclaims the heap memory allocated for that object.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Automatic Reference Counting

questions.prompt: Why do Swift structs not use reference counting, and what happens when a struct contains a class property? Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that structs are value types copied on assignment and therefore have no reference count of their own.
Explains that ARC tracks the reference count of any embedded class property when the struct is copied or destroyed.
Notes that copying the struct retains the underlying class instance.

questions.modelAnswer: Structs are value types copied upon assignment, so they have no reference count of their own. When a struct holds a property of class type, ARC manages that class instance reference count. Copying the struct adds a strong reference to the underlying class, and destroying the struct releases it.
